name: Carla Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a site supervisor and lead carpenter for Northgate Interiors. We do fit-outs, so someone builds the empty shell of an office or a shop, and we come in and make it usable: partition walls, suspended ceilings, doors, the reception desk, the kitchen. This month it's three floors of a bank's new office in the business park. I've got eleven people under me, I start at seven with a walk-round, and most days I'm half on the tools and half on the phone to the client's project manager.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's that balance like, tools and phone?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the tools more, but I'm better on the phone than I used to be. I use one of those AI chat things now and then to tidy up an email when a client's being difficult, because my first draft is usually too honest. The tools part is where I relax. Give me a door to hang and a quiet corner and I'm happy for an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a handy tool, not a miracle. I'd say it at work in a normal voice. Nobody on my sites is losing sleep over AI anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit relieved, because fit-out is repetitive in places. Studs, boards, ceiling grid, again and again. I'd always wondered if that bit was going to a machine one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Finish the bank's three floors by March, keep using the chat thing for emails, and get Erin through her exams. Maybe finally book the holiday we put off last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a weather warning that came to nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bit of your work did you think might go to a machine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Boarding. Putting plasterboard on a stud wall, sheet after sheet, the same screws, the same spacing. I've seen a video of a robot doing it in Japan. If it's all hype, my boarders keep their jobs, and I'd be glad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at home would care most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dan, my husband. He does IT support at the hospital and he's more worried about AI than I am. Half his job is resetting passwords. He'd be the one opening a bottle of wine.

S0.say: Fair enough, it's a handy tool, not a miracle. I'd say it at work in a normal voice, because nobody on my sites is losing sleep over AI anyway.
S0.think: I'd be a bit relieved, because fit-out is repetitive in places, like studs, boards and ceiling grid. I'd always wondered if that part would go to a machine.
S0.do: Finishes the bank's three office floors by March and keeps using the chatbot for emails. Supports her daughter through exams and books the holiday the family postponed last year.
S0.feel: Calm, like a weather warning that came to nothing.
S0.quote: If it's all hype, my boarders keep their jobs, and I'd be glad.
S0.fieldNote: Carla is quietly aware that parts of fit-out work, like boarding, are repetitive enough to automate. She uses AI lightly for emails. Her husband's IT job is more exposed than hers, and that shapes the household's worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change how we work, and we'd better keep up. Not panicky, just practical. I'd tell my team the same in the Monday meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my boarders and ceiling fixers are the ones in the firing line. Me, I'd probably end up running machines and people both. And Dan's job worries me more than mine, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a couple of firms used the new kit, then push Northgate to try it, so we don't fall behind. I'd use the AI for planning and quotes more, once I'd seen it work. And I'd tell Dan to start looking at what IT jobs look like in three years, because I'd want one of us to be safe. We'd start putting an extra hundred a month aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just alert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marcus. He's my best boarder, twenty-six, fast as anything, and boarding is all he does. I'd sit him down and tell him to learn the setting-out side, the measuring and marking, because that's harder to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'wait until a couple of firms use it'. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first firm always pays for the mistakes. I saw a firm buy a fancy new ceiling system five years ago, and it took them a year to make it work. I'd rather learn from their year than lose mine.

S1.say: It's going to change how we work and we'd better keep up, practical rather than panicky. I'd tell my team the same in the Monday meeting.
S1.think: My boarders and ceiling fixers are in the firing line, and I'd probably end up running machines and people both. My husband's IT job worries me more than mine.
S1.do: Waits for a couple of firms to prove new kit, then pushes Northgate to adopt it, and uses AI more for planning and quotes. Encourages her husband to look at future IT roles and sets aside an extra 100 a month.
S1.feel: Uneasy and alert, but not scared.
S1.quote: I'd rather learn from their year than lose mine.
S1.fieldNote: Carla thinks in terms of her team and spots who is most exposed. She'd adopt new tools only once others had absorbed the early mistakes. Her worry about her husband's job is stronger than her worry about her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and somebody has to slow it down. I'm not one for marches, but I'd say the government needs to get a grip. I'd say it at work and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this one is bad for us. Dan and I both go in the same two years. We've got about three months of savings, a mortgage, and a fifteen-year-old who wants to go to university. That's not a plan, that's a problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, we'd cut everything we could: the holiday, the takeaways, Max's new bike would wait. I'd move as much as I could into savings. I'd talk to Northgate about getting into whatever role runs the machines, even if it's less money. And I'd tell Dan to look right now at hospital jobs that need a person in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like reading a letter from the bank you didn't expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Erin about university?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to still apply. Then I'd lie awake doing the maths. She's always wanted to study nursing, and that might be one of the better bets in this picture, which is strange to think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take less money to run the machines. How much less could you take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a fifth. Any more and the mortgage wobbles. If Dan's job went too, there's no amount less I could take. That's the bit I can't get past.

S2.say: It's too fast and somebody has to slow it down. I'm not one for marches, but I'd say at work that the government needs to get a grip.
S2.think: This one is bad for us, because my husband and I both lose work in the same two years. We have about three months saved, a mortgage and a daughter heading for university.
S2.do: Cuts the holiday, takeaways and her son's new bike, and moves everything she can into savings. Asks Northgate for a role running the machines even at about a fifth less pay, and urges her husband to look at hospital jobs that need a person in the room.
S2.feel: Sick, like an unexpected letter from the bank.
S2.quote: That's not a plan, that's a problem.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year window alarms her because both incomes are exposed at once. She has done the maths precisely: she can take about a fifth less pay and no more. She is not political by nature but still wants government to act.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but doable, if we start now. I'd say it to the lads, and I'd tell them to get their heads round the new stuff early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me enough time to move up rather than out. I think I could become the person who plans the job and manages the robots, but I'd need to learn properly. Dan's the bigger question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a project management course at the college, evenings, starting next year. I'd use the AI tools every day once Northgate brought them in, not just now and then. We'd save a steady two hundred a month and pay off the car loan early. Dan would retrain too, maybe into hospital equipment maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way that gets me moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you fit an evening course in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Max has football Tuesdays and Thursdays, so the course would have to be Mondays and Wednesdays. Dan would do dinners. It'd be a squeeze, but we did it when the kids were small and I was doing my supervisor's ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your team in that five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them: you've got time, use it. Marcus especially. I'd help him find a course and push him onto it, because he'd never push himself.

S3.say: Five years is tight but doable if we start now. I'd tell the lads to get their heads round the new stuff early.
S3.think: Five years is enough time to move up rather than out, becoming the person who plans jobs and manages the robots. But I'd need to learn properly, and my husband is the bigger question.
S3.do: Starts an evening project management course next year and uses AI tools daily once Northgate brings them in. Saves 200 a month and pays off the car loan early, while her husband retrains in hospital equipment maintenance.
S3.feel: Anxious in a way that gets her moving.
S3.quote: Five years gives me enough time to move up rather than out.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her plan a step up into managing work rather than doing it. Her steady style still shows in retraining at a measured pace. She keeps thinking about her best boarder, Marcus, and wants to push him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years, so let's be sensible about it. I'd say it in a work chat and leave it there, I don't get into arguments online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is enough to retrain at my own pace. I'd be fifty-three when it lands, Erin would be out of uni, Max nearly there. We'd be okay if we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch for a couple of years, see what the big firms do, then retrain properly, probably into project management or inspection. We'd overpay the mortgage a bit every month. And I'd talk to Max about what he wants to do, because he'd be leaving school right into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more like I'm planning a move than facing a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Max?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Max loves fixing things, bikes, the lawnmower. I'd say keep fixing things, but learn how the machines are built, not just how to use them. Someone's always going to have to fix the robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd regret in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that the hands-on part goes. I'd miss hanging a door in a quiet corner. But I've always said, you don't love a job, you love what it gets you, and I'd find something else that gets me the same.

S4.say: We've got ten years, so let's be sensible about it. I'd say that in a work chat and leave it, because I don't get into arguments online.
S4.think: Ten years is enough to retrain at my own pace, and by then my daughter would be out of university and my son nearly there. We'd be okay if we planned.
S4.do: Watches for two years to see what the big firms do, then retrains in project management or inspection. Overpays the mortgage a little each month and talks with her son about his options.
S4.feel: Uneasy, more like planning a move than facing a storm.
S4.quote: Someone's always going to have to fix the robot.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years her worry eases into planning. She would still wait to see proof before retraining, which is her habit. Her advice to her son about fixing the robots mirrors her own practical streak.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Dan and I both go at once and there's no time to plan. What would help is something to keep the mortgage paid for a year or two, while we retrain, and courses that actually lead to jobs, not just certificates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the partners. Everyone asks about my job, but what keeps me up is the two jobs together. If one of us is safe, we're fine. If neither of us is, I don't know what we'd do.

headlineQuote: If one of us is safe, we're fine. If neither of us is, I don't know what we'd do.
portrait: Carla Walsh is a 43-year-old site supervisor and lead carpenter for a commercial fit-out firm, currently on a bank's new offices, married to a hospital IT worker, with two children and about three months saved. She uses a chatbot now and then to soften her emails and would adopt new tools once other firms had proven them. She's calm under a plateau and uneasy under steady change, aware that boarding and ceiling work are repetitive. The two-year AGI picture alarms her because both household jobs would go at once, while five or ten years give her time to retrain into project management or inspection.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and her husband would both lose work at once with no time to plan.
whatWouldHelp: Help keeping the mortgage paid for a year or two while they retrain, and courses that lead to real jobs.
